Article Title: Safety vs privacy: How domestic-help platforms are building a two-way support system
Article Text:
A significant demographic of the service providers at these platforms and the consumers comprise of women.

Formalising trust in an informal workforce

Safety vs surveillance divide

Safety by design

What women check before opening the door

The rituals of being home alone

The older customer’s definition of trust

The next phase of trust

India’s instant domestic help economy is expanding faster. App-based platforms promise cleaners, cooks and household workers within minutes. However, the real contest here is no longer just about speed, convenience or pricing. It is increasingly about trust.A significant demographic of the service providers at these platforms and the consumers comprises women.For years, domestic work in India has operated through informal neighbourhood networks, word-of-mouth referrals and personal recommendations. The new generation of platforms is attempting to formalise that ecosystem by adding identity verification, digital payments, ratings, training, insurance and customer support.But unlike food delivery or ride-hailing, these services involve something far more intimate: a stranger entering a private home.That has forced platforms to solve an unusually difficult problem. They must simultaneously protect women who enter unfamiliar homes for work and women who may be home alone when they invite those workers inside.The result is a rapidly evolving safety architecture built around background checks, restricted service hours, real-time monitoring, SOS systems, human escalation teams and, increasingly, AI-assisted risk detection.India’s domestic work sector employs millions of workers, many of them women, and remains overwhelmingly informal. Instant domestic help platforms have created new income opportunities by offering structured onboarding, predictable payments and access to a larger customer base.But formalisation has also brought safety concerns into sharper focus.A spokesperson for Pronto shared the measures it takes to ensure transparency, saying that every worker completes criminal court record verification and police verification before joining the platform. Customers, too, verify their name, phone number and address through OTP authentication and must agree to a code of conduct before placing a booking.Pronto's workers, for example, receive training before taking their first assignment, and that low customer ratings are investigated by trainers rather than triggering automatic deactivation.“Every hub we operate doubles as a training centre, and a professional takes her first booking only after she is trained, background-verified and dispatch-ready, a process that takes about four days,” the spokesperson said.Similarly, Snabbit, whose workforce consists entirely of women professionals, said it has built a multi-layered safety framework supported by a dedicated Trust & Safety team.A spokesperson said the system includes “mandatory KYC and background checks for all experts on the platform, verified customers, address-level traceability and controlled job allocation.”The sharpest divide between platforms and customers is emerging around body-worn cameras.Pronto has begun experimenting with optional recorded bookings designed to protect workers from false allegations in cases of disputes with customers.For many users, however, the presence of a camera inside a private home changes the nature of the interaction. “I know some platforms are starting to equip their workers with chest-mounted bodycams for transparency, and while I understand it protects the worker from false claims, it completely freaks me out as a customer,” a Delhi resident said.“My home is my private sanctuary. The idea of a stranger walking through my living room with an active lens, recording the exact layout of my home, my entrances, my exits, my personal belongings, and where my work setup or valuables are, feels like an extreme invasion of privacy.”Her concerns extend beyond the recording itself. “Where is that video footage stored? Who at the tech company has access to it? Could that footage leak or be hacked?” she said. “I would honestly think twice before booking a service that mandates live video recording inside my private space. There has to be a boundary between physical safety and digital surveillance.”Pronto, however, ensured that the sole mechanism of this process is to ensure safety and privacy.It said that additional video data is collected only on opt-in verified bookings. According to its spokesperson, customers choose the feature during booking and confirm it again when the worker arrives. The camera is tilted downward to capture only the work area, records no audio, blurs faces and personal information on the device itself, deletes raw footage immediately, and retains only an anonymised encrypted version for a limited review period and AI training.One of the most striking trends across the sector is that many safety measures are designed not around responding to incidents, but around preventing high-risk situations from arising in the first place.Several platforms have restricted service hours, particularly avoiding late-evening and night bookings when women workers may be required to enter unfamiliar homes after dark.Snabbit said its safety system monitors active jobs in real time and can identify anomalies that may require intervention. According to its spokesperson, “Active jobs are monitored in real time, with the dedicated Trust & Safety team supporting rapid escalation and incident response.”For many women, however, trust begins long before a worker arrives.A 24-year-old student in Jaipur said she has developed a consistent checklist before booking any on-demand domestic service. She checks whether the app displays a verified profile with a photograph, ID verification, ratings and reviews, and prefers platforms that offer real-time tracking and OTP-based service verification.“The first thing I check is whether the app shows a verified profile with a photo, ID verification, ratings, and reviews from other women,” she said. “Real-time tracking and an OTP-based start and end of the service also make me feel more comfortable.”Before the worker arrives, she follows a set of precautions that have become almost automatic. She keeps her phone fully charged, informs at least one friend that someone is coming over, avoids leaving valuables or personal documents in plain sight, and stays in a part of the house where she can easily monitor what is happening.“I usually make sure my phone is fully charged and I let at least one friend know that someone is coming over,” she said. “If it’s a longer service, I stay in a part of the house where I can easily see what’s happening.”She is also careful about digital privacy. “I prefer apps that mask phone numbers, and I never share extra details unless they’re necessary for the service,” she said. “I avoid mentioning that I live alone or discussing my schedule. Once the job is done, I’m careful not to continue communication outside the platform.”For her, safety is not just about preventing a crime; it is about minimising information that could make her vulnerable later.Minal, a 26-year-old professional in Delhi described a different set of habits that have emerged through repeated use of instant service platforms. While the agent is at home, she stays in the hall rather than a closed bedroom, keeps her phone in her hand, and deliberately leaves a pair of her partner’s or male flatmate’s shoes near the entrance.“I never sit in my bedroom with the door shut. I stay in the main living area, usually at the dining table with my laptop,” she said. “I also leave a pair of my male flatmate’s or partner’s shoes near the entryway. It’s a small mental trick, but it makes me feel less exposed.”She and two close friends have an informal safety protocol built around messaging apps.“I have a private WhatsApp group with two close friends. We have a tacit rule: whenever an instant maid or repair person is assigned, I drop the tracking link, their name, and a quick ‘Expected time: 45 mins,’” she said. “I don’t overthink it, but it gives me a safety net.”When asked what app features actually make her feel secure, she was sceptical of marketing labels.“Honestly, badges and ‘police verified’ tags on an app screen don’t mean much to me anymore. Anyone can upload a document,” she said. “What actually makes me feel safe is seeing a real-time, live selfie of the person taken right when they accept the job, matching the photo on their profile. Plus, knowing there’s a strict OTP entry system where they can’t start billing until I give them a code at the door.”Her distinction is important: she is less interested in historical verification and more interested in real-time authentication.For older users, digital verification often feels less persuasive than physical verification. Sarita , a 52-year-old homemaker in Delhi-NCR, said she places greater trust in tangible indicators such as uniforms, identity cards and residential security systems.“A professional now gets to share her version of events and any relevant information before a decision is taken, and we work to keep investigations balanced and transparent,” Pronto spokesperson said.That shift, from treating workers merely as service providers to treating them as rights-bearing participants in the platform ecosystem, may prove as important as any technological innovation.As instant domestic help services expand beyond metropolitan cities into smaller urban centres, safety may become the industry’s primary competitive differentiator.Speed is easy to advertise. Trust is harder to build.Women are asking for features that combine digital verification with human accountability: live identity confirmation, female-worker filters, trusted-contact notifications, residential gate integration, discreet exit mechanisms, neighbourhood-level reputation and transparent data governance.Platforms, meanwhile, are investing in training hubs, background verification, restricted service hours, SOS networks, counselling, insurance and AI-assisted monitoring.
Article Summary: India’s domestic work sector employs millions of workers, many of them women, and remains overwhelmingly informal. Instant domestic help platforms have created new income opportunities by offering structured onboarding, predictable payments and access to a larger customer base. But formalisation has also brought safety concerns into sharper focus.

Article Title: Scientists use AI to create new viruses; bringing worries of the tech creating biological weapons, deadly poisons and unstoppable pandemics
Article Text:
An atomic reconstruction of one of the bacteriophages designed by the Evo AI model. (Image credit: Samuel H. King et al.)

How AI learned to write DNA like it writes sentences

How scientists confirmed the AI-designed viruses were actually alive

What the researchers did to keep this from going wrong

The gap between what AI can do and what anyone regulates

Poll Vote & Share your view What fascinates you most about AI designing organisms? Potential for medical breakthroughs The technology behind it The ethical implications The novelty of the concept 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Scientists have used artificial intelligence to design viruses that exist nowhere in nature, and 16 of them turned out to be fully functional killers of bacteria. The work, published Thursday in the journal Science by a team at Stanford University and the Arc Institute in California, is the first time an AI model has written the complete instruction manual for a living thing rather than just one piece of it. The viruses in question only attack bacteria and cannot infect people, animals or plants.That last bit is the reassuring part, and everyone involved knows how thin it sounds. The same study that promises a new weapon against superbugs also proves that software trained on DNA can now dream up a working virus from a blank page. Two researchers at Johns Hopkins, Thomas Inglesby and Moritz Hanke, put it plainly in a commentary published alongside it: the ability to write viral genomes with AI now exists, and the rules to control it do not.The models, called Evo 1 and Evo 2, work a lot like ChatGPT. ChatGPT guesses which word comes next. Evo guesses which chemical letter comes next in a strand of DNA, which uses an alphabet of just four letters: A, C, G and T. Feed it enough genetic code and it starts picking up the grammar of life the way a chatbot picks up English.The team, led by Stanford's Brian Hie, trained it on millions of natural genomes, then focused it on one very well-studied virus called ΦX174 and its relatives.Evo spat out hundreds of thousands of possible designs. The researchers picked around 300, had the DNA physically made in a lab, and slipped it into bacteria—which obediently read the instructions and built the viruses themselves.Graduate student Samuel King spotted it in the early hours of the morning. Bacteria growing on a petri dish form a cloudy film, and when a virus is chewing through them, clear spots appear. The spots appeared. When he told the rest of the team, Hie recalls, "the room spontaneously burst into applause."The 16 that survived were not weak imitations. Some multiplied faster than the natural virus they were modelled on. And in the most useful result of the lot, a mix of the AI-designed viruses wiped out E. coli that had already learned to resist the natural version. A comparable mix of viruses collected from nature could not. Bacteria evolve to survive whatever we throw at them—this suggests we can now design new threats faster than they can adapt.They kept anything dangerous out of the training data. No viruses that infect humans, animals, plants or fungi went in, so the model has never seen what a human pathogen looks like. They used a harmless strain of E. coli and worked in a secure lab. Hanke called the caution commendable, while noting the team had no official rulebook to follow.A new US health policy issued last week bans making biological agents more dangerous, but it doesn't cover work done on a computer. And Evo 2 is open source, free for anyone to download, which has alarmed plenty of people.Others say the panic is early. Tom Ellis at Imperial College London called this the smallest, simplest genome anyone could have attempted. Size backs him up: this virus needs about 5,400 letters of code. The simplest living cell needs 500,000. Hie says going bigger would be "a lot of work, but not impossible"—which isn't exactly comforting.
Article Summary: Scientists have used artificial intelligence to design viruses that exist nowhere in nature. 16 of them turned out to be fully functional killers of bacteria. The work is the first time an AI model has written the complete instruction manual for a living thing. The viruses in question only attack bacteria and cannot infect people, animals or plants.

Article Title: Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's $450 million superyacht hides a secret sea cabin deep inside the hull, designed to reduce seasickness and ensure peaceful sleep during rough voyages
Article Text:
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman Al Saud’s 439-foot Serene one of the most fascinating bedrooms sits three decks below the owner’s suite.

Using naval design to reduce motion

The Balinese inspired cabin. Image – charterworld

Simple Balinese design with practical features

Designer Pascale Reymond once described it as one of the yacht’s coolest ideas (Image – charter​world)

Italian craftsmanship and luxury features

To escape the scorching summer heat of the Middle East, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman Al Saud equipped his $450 million superyacht Serene with a custom-built snow room cooled to minus 11 degrees Celsius. But despite the yacht's luxurious features, one of its most important design elements is hidden three decks below the main owner's suite.Located near the exact centre of the 439-foot yacht, a secret Balinese-inspired "sea cabin" was specially designed to reduce seasickness and provide a peaceful place to sleep during rough sea journeys.While many billionaire yacht owners place their master bedrooms high up for the best views, Serene has a two-master layout based on how ships move. Reports have long linked the Crown Prince to seasickness during long trips across the Mediterranean and open oceans. Instead of relying only on the yacht's powerful stabilisers, the designers used the science of ship movement to create a calmer sleeping space when the sea becomes rough.The sea cabin is located on the starboard side near the middle of Deck Two, one of the most stable positions on the 134-metre yacht.Naval architecture explains why this location is so effective during voyages. The front of a ship rises and falls heavily in waves, while the rear is affected by pitching, engine vibrations and movement caused by the propellers. Higher decks also move much more from side to side as the yacht rolls.By placing the cabin low in the hull near the centre, the room stays close to the yacht's natural balance points, where movement is at its lowest. Serene is fitted with advanced active stabilisers that greatly reduce rolling, but no system can remove all movement during storms or long ocean crossings. For people who suffer from seasickness, sleeping in the middle of the yacht can make a significant difference.Inside, the sea cabin focuses on calm, simple luxury rather than flashy decoration, creating the feel of a tropical beach retreat. A double bed faces the rear of the yacht beneath a ceiling designed to look like the underside of a traditional Balinese thatched roof. Natural colours, modern furnishings and a floor-to-ceiling headboard separate the bedroom from the open bathroom.One of the cabin's standout features is a large shell door built into the side of the yacht. When Serene is anchored, the door folds down to become a private balcony at sea level, allowing guests to step directly onto the water. During voyages, the balcony stays securely closed, allowing the cabin to serve its main purpose as a stable bedroom.Designer Pascale Reymond once described the cabin as one of the yacht's best ideas because "it's so earthy." Its location is also highly practical. A guest kitchen sits next door, allowing the owner to prepare a late-night snack without calling crew members or climbing several flights of stairs. The spa and beach club are just a short walk away, while a private lift connects the cabin directly to the main owner's suite on Deck Five. This gives the Crown Prince a spacious suite for relaxing in calm waters and a quieter, more stable room for sleeping at sea.Built by Italian shipyard Fincantieri and launched in 2011, Serene is one of the largest and most advanced superyachts ever constructed in Italy. The yacht measures 439 feet (134 metres) long with a beam of 60.7 feet (18.5 metres). Its exterior was designed by Espen Øino, while the interiors were created by Reymond Langton Design. According to Charter World, Serene is powered by eight MTU 4000-series engines, cruises comfortably at 15 knots, reaches a top speed of 20 knots, accommodates 24 guests in 12 cabins, and is operated by a crew of 52.Besides its special sea cabin, Serene offers an impressive range of luxury facilities across seven decks. The yacht has two helicopter landing pads, one of which can be turned into a swimming pool or dance floor, a submarine hangar, and an underwater viewing lounge called the Nemo Room, inspired by Jules Verne's Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea.To help guests escape the region's extreme heat, the yacht also includes a snow room cooled to around 12 degrees Fahrenheit (-11°C). The room creates real falling snow, allowing guests to move directly into a nearby sauna, hammam, steam room or heated spa pools. With an indoor seawater swimming pool, an outdoor cinema, a piano lounge and domed fireplaces, Serene combines luxury with smart engineering to handle both extreme heat and rough seas.
Article Summary: Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman Al Saud's 439-foot superyacht Serene has a secret Balinese-inspired "sea cabin" The cabin was designed to reduce seasickness and provide a peaceful place to sleep during rough sea journeys. It is located on the starboard side near the middle of Deck Two, one of the most stable positions on the 134-metre yacht.

Article Title: Apple releases macOS Tahoe 26.6.1 to fix Screen Sharing security flaw
Article Text:
Mac users can check for the latest update in the Settings app

How to download macOS Tahoe 26.6.1

Apple's most popular Mac is now its hardest to buy

Apple has released macOS Tahoe 26.6.1, a new security update for Mac users that fixes a vulnerability related to the Screen Sharing feature. According to Apple’s security support document, the flaw could allow an attacker to authenticate to Screen Sharing without having valid credentials. Apple says it has addressed the security issue by improving state management. The company has also released updates for older macOS versions, including macOS Sonoma 14.8.9 and macOS Sequoia 15.7.9, with the same security fix.The fix is not limited to Macs running macOS Tahoe. Apple has also released macOS Sonoma 14.8.9 and macOS Sequoia 15.7.9, which address the same Screen Sharing vulnerability. This means Mac users who have not upgraded to macOS Tahoe can also install the security fix while remaining on their existing supported macOS version.Mac users can check for the latest update by opening the System Settings app and navigating to the Software Update section. If macOS Tahoe 26.6.1 is available for the device, users can download and install it from there.Given that the update addresses a security vulnerability that could allow authentication without valid credentials, users may want to install the latest available update on their Macs.In another news, shipping estimates of Apple MacBook Air have slipped by weeks across nearly every configuration, likely because of the global memory shortage. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reported in his Power On newsletter that retail sources describe Air inventory as more constrained than they can ever recall. Order a base model from Apple's online store today and delivery lands at the end of August. Buyers of the Apple MacBook Air are reportedly being told to wait till early September to get hold of the device.
Article Summary: macOS Tahoe 26.6.1 is a new security update for Mac users that fixes a vulnerability related to the Screen Sharing feature. The flaw could allow an attacker to authenticate to Screen Sharing without having valid credentials. Apple has also released updates for older macOS versions, including macOS Sonoma 14.8.9 and macOS Sequoia 15.7.9.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works







Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness.

Article Title: PhD candidates allege bribery, harassment by some staffers at Babasaheb Ambedkar Marathwada University
Article Text:
The allegations have drawn strong criticism from members of the university senate

Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar

:





A section of PhD candidates at the Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar Marathwada University (Bamu) has alleged that staff members in the university’s PhD section demand bribes and deliberately delay academic processes, including thesis submission and evaluation-related formalities.Candidates claim they are forced to make repeated visits to the section and face harassment if they refuse to pay money. “We have to make multiple visits to the PhD section and some staffers demand Rs 500 to Rs 1,000 to speed up pending work. Those unwilling to pay are often asked to come again on one pretext or another,” alleged a PhD scholar in microbiology.Another candidate pursuing a PhD in environmental science claimed that such practices have become routine. “Bribery and harassment have become a norm at the PhD section. Research scholars are already burdened with academic work and such a toxic atmosphere only adds to their difficulties,” he said.The allegations have drawn strong criticism from members of the university senate.Narendra Kale, a Bamu senate member, alleged that some staffers create unnecessary hurdles in thesis submission and forwarding dissertations to external experts.“As per many candidates, unnecessary delays and hurdles are created in submitting theses and sending them to experts. Candidates are afraid of raising their voice against such staffers,” Kale said, warning that an agitation would be launched if the situation was not addressed.Bamu offers PhD programmes in more than 30 subjects across its four faculties and witnesses a large number of aspirants appearing for its entrance examinations every year.Vice-Chancellor Dr Vijay Phulari did not respond to requests for comment.
Article Summary: Candidates claim they are forced to make repeated visits to the section and face harassment if they refuse to pay money. The allegations have drawn strong criticism from members of the university senate. Vice-Chancellor Dr Vijay Phulari did not respond to requests for comment.

Article Title: Spain's blood-red Río Tinto river is as acidic as vinegar, and Nasa says it could help scientists find life on Mars
Article Text:
PC: David Santiago Garcia/Aurora Photos/Getty Images

Why Spain's Río Tinto river is naturally blood red and as acidic as vinegar

How extremophiles thrive in Spain's highly acidic Río Tinto river

How 5,000 years of mining shaped Spain's famous blood-red river

Why Nasa studies Spain's Río Tinto river to search for life on Mars

At first glance, the Río Tinto in southwestern Spain looks almost unreal. For around 50 kilometres, the water flows in shades of deep red and orange that seem more fitting for an artist's palette than a natural river. Yet its extraordinary appearance is not the result of artificial dyes or recent contamination. It reflects a landscape shaped by ancient geology, microscopic organisms and thousands of years of mining. What appears to be an environment too harsh to support life has instead become home to specialised microbes that thrive where most living things cannot. According to Nasa, those unusual conditions make the Río Tinto one of the closest natural environments on Earth to parts of Mars, giving scientists a rare opportunity to test how they might one day detect life beyond our planet.The Río Tinto, whose name translates as "stained river", cuts through one of Europe's richest volcanic sulfide ore regions. These mineral deposits formed hundreds of millions of years ago when volcanic activity dominated what is now southern Spain.As groundwater and oxygen reach those buried sulfide minerals, a chain of chemical reactions begins. Iron and sulfur compounds dissolve into the water, making it highly acidic.Bacterial communities living within the river do not simply tolerate these conditions, they actively contribute to them by oxidising iron and sulfur compounds. In doing so, they produce ferric iron, the rust-coloured material responsible for the river's striking red appearance.The river's acidity is remarkable. Its pH can fall to around 2, roughly comparable with vinegar, creating an environment where most familiar plants, fish and other aquatic organisms struggle to survive.Despite those hostile conditions, the Río Tinto is far from lifeless. Instead, it supports communities of extremophiles, organisms specially adapted to environments that would prove fatal to most other forms of life. These microbes obtain energy by processing iron and sulfur rather than relying on sunlight or organic matter in the way many other ecosystems do. Their activity also reinforces the river's unusual chemistry, maintaining the acidic conditions that define the ecosystem.Scientists regard these organisms as particularly valuable because they demonstrate that life can flourish in places once thought too extreme to support it. Rather than seeing acidity as an obstacle, these microbes have evolved to use the river's unusual chemical environment as part of their survival strategy.Although the Río Tinto's chemistry has natural origins, people have influenced the landscape for millennia. Archaeological evidence indicates mining in the region stretches back around 5,000 years, spanning the Copper Age, Bronze Age and later Roman activity. Centuries of excavation exposed increasing amounts of sulfide-rich rock to air and water, amplifying processes that were already occurring naturally. Modern industrial mining continued until operations were suspended in 2001 before copper production resumed in 2016.For many years, the river's unusual colour was widely attributed solely to mining pollution. Empowering rural communities through sustainable land stewardship

On a sun-soaked slope in Zvishavane, Zimbabwe, small farmer Zephaniah Phiri Maseko took stock of his degraded land in the 1960s and made up his mind to do something about it. Where others were suffering from erosion and watching their scarce water supplies being washed away by rain flowing downhill, Maseko seems to have realised the importance of collecting water where it fell to assure his long-term sustenance. He embarked on an elaborate exercise of digging a series of shallow pits, bunds, and terraces all around his land, with the sole objective of holding back the rapid flow of surface water and letting it percolate underground.Rather than allowing rain to sweep away fertile topsoil, Maseko turned much of his farm into a water-retaining landscape. Residents originally thought his elaborate earthworks were an exercise in futility, but the results suggested otherwise. As the years went on, Maseko successfully elevated the local water table beneath his property. Even during regional droughts, Maseko's water-harvesting system helped keep his hand-dug wells supplied, allowing his family to continue growing fruit trees, vegetables, and grain crops when water became scarce on many neighbouring farms.The broader importance of local ecological knowledge in farming is explored in the study Farmers' Knowledge and Perception of Agricultural Wetlands in Rwanda by agricultural scientists N. L. Nabahungu and S. M. Visser.The research examined how rural communities understand and manage wetland landscapes, including how farmers classify areas based on drainage conditions and match crops to different moisture levels. Although the study focused on wetlands rather than dry hillside water harvesting, it highlights a similar principle seen in Maseko’s work: farmers often rely on detailed observations of their surroundings to make decisions about water and land management.Maseko’s strategy focused on working with the natural shape of the landscape rather than relying on external irrigation systems. He designed swales and earthen embankments along contour lines to slow rainwater as it moved downhill, allowing more water to infiltrate the soil. The captured water gradually permeated the soil and recharged groundwater resources. The subterranean water supported the growth of deeply-rooted vegetation even in dry seasons when the first rains passed.Over several decades, Maseko expanded his water-harvesting system, creating earthworks that helped capture and slow rainwater runoff during storms, allowing more water to soak into the soil. This water infiltration improved soil conditions on his hillside, helping turn dry, compacted clay into richer soil. Surrounding vegetation reportedly improved, which may have attracted more wildlife and livestock. The hillside became more productive, suggesting that water harvesting can help restore degraded land.Beyond securing household water independence, Maseko’s methods offered a low-cost, sustainable model for smallholder farmers across semi-arid regions of Africa. His farm became a world-renowned training centre, drawing thousands of visiting agriculturalists, researchers, and local farmers eager to learn how to harvest rainfall on their own lands. By relying on simple hand tools and local materials, Maseko demonstrated that dramatic ecological restoration does not require heavy machinery or massive financial capital.The experiences of Maseko demonstrate how localised water retention methods could enhance water availability at the small farm level. On the other hand, the research work carried out by Nabahungu and Visser has brought out the role of farmers in managing water resources using their indigenous knowledge base.The lessons from Farmers' Knowledge and Perception of Agricultural Wetlands in Rwanda confirm the significance of incorporating traditional agricultural knowledge in environmental management programs. Nabahungu and Visser’s study revealed that knowledge of local wetlands among farmers is critical in managing their agricultural landscape.The study highlighted the importance of understanding local landscapes and farmers’ ecological knowledge when managing agricultural environments. When farmers manage surface runoff on hillsides, they can reduce erosion, limit siltation and support groundwater recharge across the catchment area. This holistic perspective mirrors Maseko’s core philosophy that managing water on the heights is essential for sustaining life in the valleys below.Years down the line, even after Maseko used the shovel for the first time to break the ground in the dry area of Zvishavane, his work still inspires many people in drought management and agroecology. Harvesting surface water on the contour slopes is still an applicable practice for small-scale farmers at the moment.

Article Title: Inside the US town where cell phones barely work because scientists are listening to the universe
Article Text:
Representative Image of a radio-quiet mountain town where wireless signals are heavily restricted (AI-generated image)

Why this specific stretch of Appalachia went radio silent

Why the telescope is sensitive enough to need this much protection

How two separate layers of legal restriction actually work

How officials actually monitor and enforce these restrictions

Why some people have chosen to move to the quiet zone deliberately

Why Green Bank remains scientifically important today

In the mountains of eastern West Virginia sits Green Bank, a town of roughly 150 people where using a cell phone, running a Wi-Fi router, or operating a microwave near the town centre is not just impractical; it is against the law. Green Bank sits at the heart of the National Radio Quiet Zone, a 13,000 square mile region spanning much of eastern West Virginia and parts of Virginia, established in 1958 to protect one of the most sensitive scientific instruments in the country, the Robert C Byrd Green Bank Telescope, the world's largest fully steerable radio telescope, from the interference of ordinary modern wireless technology.According to the Green Bank Observatory, the National Radio Quiet Zone was formally established by the Federal Communications Commission in November 1958, working alongside the federal Interdepartment Radio Advisory Committee, specifically to minimise harmful radio interference to the National Radio Astronomy Observatory in Green Bank and a separate United States Navy receiving facility located at Sugar Grove, West Virginia. According to the observatory's own history, the site itself was chosen a few years earlier, with construction of the original National Radio Astronomy Observatory beginning in 1956 after a 1954 meeting in Washington, DC first raised the idea of establishing a dedicated national centre for radio astronomy in the United States.The zone's boundaries are precisely defined by longitude and latitude coordinates rather than following any natural or state border, and according to the observatory, it encloses an area of approximately 13,000 square miles straddling the state line between Virginia and West Virginia, one of the largest radio restricted zones of its kind anywhere in the world.The reasoning behind such an extensive restricted zone comes down to just how faint the signals researchers are trying to detect actually are. According to Green Bank Observatory, astronomers measure incoming radio signals in units called Jansky, and the telescope frequently detects signals measured in milli- or even micro-Janskys, decimal fractions so small that the observatory describes the energy involved as less than that of a single snowflake landing on the ground. By this measure, a single ordinary cell phone, even one located as far away as Mars, would still register on the telescope's instruments with far more energy than many of the faint cosmic signals researchers are actually trying to study.Because the telescope is designed to detect exactly this kind of extraordinarily weak signal, even minor local radio frequency interference from everyday consumer electronics can effectively drown out genuine astronomical data, making strict control over nearby transmissions a scientific necessity rather than simple caution.Rather than operating under a single blanket rule, protection for the observatory works through two overlapping legal frameworks. According to Green Bank Observatory, the wider 13,000 square mile National Radio Quiet Zone requires that any new or modified permanent, fixed radio transmitter within its boundaries be formally coordinated with federal regulators before installation, a rule enforced primarily through required federal licensing coordination rather than an outright ban across the entire zone.Closer to the telescope itself, a considerably stricter rule applies. The West Virginia Radio Astronomy Zoning Act, codified in the state's own legal code, makes it illegal to operate, or cause to be operated, any electrical equipment that causes harmful interference with radio wave reception within a graduated area extending up to 10 miles from the observatory's telescopes, with the most severe restrictions concentrated within the innermost few miles surrounding the site itself.Keeping the zone genuinely quiet requires ongoing, active monitoring rather than a rule that simply exists on paper. According to reporting from NPR, staff from the National Radio Astronomy Observatory drive a roughly 20-mile radius around the Green Bank Telescope on a regular basis, actively searching for equipment producing radio interference that could compromise the telescope's readings. When a source of interference is identified, observatory staff typically work directly with the equipment's owner to resolve the issue voluntarily rather than immediately pursuing legal enforcement, reflecting an approach built more around cooperation with the small local community than strict policing.This localised, hands-on enforcement stands in contrast to the far more common approach of technical, remote monitoring used to manage radio spectrum interference elsewhere in the country, underscoring just how unusual Green Bank's situation genuinely is within the broader US regulatory landscape.Green Bank's restrictions have drawn more than just scientists to the area over the years. According to NPR reporting from 2011, a small number of Americans who believe they experience physical symptoms from exposure to Wi-Fi and cell phone signals, a condition not recognised by mainstream medical science as having a demonstrated physiological basis, have relocated specifically to Green Bank and the surrounding quiet zone, drawn by the area's uniquely low levels of ambient radio frequency exposure compared to almost anywhere else in the country.For the town's more typical residents, living without reliable cell service or home Wi-Fi remains a genuine daily adjustment, one that has become increasingly unusual as connectivity has become standard virtually everywhere else in the United States, even as landline telephones, cable internet and satellite television remain available and commonly used throughout the zone.More than six decades after the National Radio Quiet Zone was first established, Green Bank continues to serve as one of the most important sites in American radio astronomy, hosting research into subjects ranging from the structure of the Milky Way to the detection of pulsars and other faint cosmic phenomena that would be effectively impossible to study amid the radio frequency noise of a typical modern town or city. For the roughly 150 people who call Green Bank home, that scientific mission has meant living, quite literally, off the grid in one specific, deliberately engineered way, a trade-off that has turned an otherwise ordinary Appalachian mountain community into one of the most electromagnetically unusual places in the entire country.
Article Summary: Green Bank, West Virginia sits at the heart of the National Radio Quiet Zone. The 13,000 square mile region was established in 1958 to protect one of the most sensitive scientific instruments in the country. The Robert C Byrd Green Bank Telescope is the world's largest fully steerable radio telescope.

Article Text:

Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.

This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

You can assign specific items to each beneficiary and select backup beneficiaries in case your first choices can't inherit. Then, choose an executor, the person who will carry out your will.Use one of the customizable templates available on the platform. Follow the instructions to fill in the details, specifying how you want your assets distributed and including any special conditions or terms.You can review the drafted will to ensure it's accurate and make changes if needed. If you have complicated issues, it's best to get legal advice. Once you're satisfied, you can legally execute the will according to the platform's rules, usually by electronically signing it with witnesses. The completed will is then stored securely online, with encryption for added security.With inputs from Centre for Investment Education and Learning content which appeared in Economic Times
Article Summary: If you are planning to create a will, many online platforms offer easy-to-use tools and resources, allowing you to draft and finalise a will without leaving your home. To register, enter your personal information like your full name, date of birth, address, and contact details. Then create a secure username and password to access the online service.

Article Title: How to get your CIBIL credit score without a PAN card
Article Text:
Your credit score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity.

What is a CIBIL score?

How to get your CIBIL Credit score without a PAN Card

Factors affecting your CIBIL score

CIBIL credit score : Understanding your creditworthiness is pivotal in today's financial landscape, especially when seeking loans or credit cards. The Credit Information Bureau (India) Limited, commonly known as CIBIL, plays an important role in this regard by providing credit scores to borrowers.According to ET, credit score helps banks make informed decisions about extending credit cards and loans. Your credit history influences your CIBIL score , which is calculated using a special method.Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.1. Go to the official CIBIL website and click on 'Personal CIBIL score,' then 'Get Your Free CIBIL score.' Follow the link provided and fill in all the required details.2. If you don’t have a PAN Card, you can use an alternative identification such as Passport, Voter ID, Driver’s License, or Ration Card. Enter the number of the chosen ID.3. Provide your date of birth, PIN code, and select your state. Finally, enter your mobile number and click on ‘Accept and Continue’.4. Authenticate your identity by entering the OTP (One-Time Password) delivered to your mobile device on the next screen. Click 'Continue' to proceed.5. Choose whether you want to link the device with your account. Select 'Yes' or 'No' based on your preference.6. Upon successful registration, you will see a page confirming that 'You have successfully registered!'7. Click on ‘Go to Dashboard’ to access and view your CIBIL score.The factors influencing the new CIBIL score, as stated on the CIBIL website, include:1. Depth of credit: This refers to the duration of your existing credit history, calculated from the opening date of your oldest credit account.2. Long-term trend of outstanding balances: The overall trend of outstanding balances over time affects your score.3. Transaction history on credit cards: How you manage transactions on your credit cards impacts your score.4. Ratio of actual repayment amount to total amount due: This ratio indicates your repayment behavior and influences your score accordingly.5. Number of new accounts opened and number of accounts closed: Opening or closing accounts can affect your score, so managing these actions wisely is important.
Article Summary: Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.

Article Title: AI is in finance, but is it ready? 76% firms use AI as governance lags, says report
Article Text:
Only 28% are reassessing the talent profiles needed for an AI-driven finance workforce.

Better AI needs better data

AI is becoming a bigger part of finance departments, but companies are finding that adopting the technology is easier than figuring out how people, data and controls should work around it.A KPMG report found that 76 per cent of organisations are already using AI in financial planning. Yet the report suggests that simply adding AI tools will not be enough to create an advantage. The bigger gains are expected to come from using AI to support better financial decisions, while building the systems and governance needed to manage its growing role."Competitive advantage will increasingly belong to organizations that align their finance operating model around AI -- and can sustain that alignment as AI becomes more capable, more autonomous and more deeply embedded in everyday decision-making."The shift is also exposing a gap in how companies are preparing their finance teams.While 38 per cent of organisations are upskilling finance and internal audit employees for AI-enabled processes, only 28 per cent are hiring for new skill sets. An identical 28 per cent are reassessing the talent profiles they will need as AI becomes more deeply integrated into finance.In other words, most organisations are teaching their existing workforce to use AI rather than redesigning the workforce around human-AI collaboration.That transition is also keeping humans firmly in the loop. KPMG found that 33 per cent of organisations are increasing human oversight specifically because of concerns linked to AI.This remains particularly important in finance, where decisions can involve regulatory requirements and professional judgement. Human checks, the report said, can make AI-driven outputs more reliable while helping organisations build confidence in the technology.Even as companies expand AI use, the quality of the underlying data remains a major constraint.About 36 per cent of organisations identified better data quality, integration and interoperability between systems as the biggest opportunity to get more value from AI in finance.The challenge, therefore, is not simply having more AI tools. Finance teams also need to understand which data can be trusted, how AI-generated outputs should be interpreted and how those findings can be translated into decisions."Data fluency is emerging as the most critical capability need: the ability to assess data quality, interpret outputs and communicate findings in terms the business can act on."The report's broader takeaway is that AI adoption alone may not determine which finance teams benefit most. Companies that combine the technology with stronger governance, appropriate talent and reliable data are likely to be better placed as AI becomes more autonomous.
Article Summary: KPMG: 76% of organisations are already using AI in financial planning. Only 28% are reassessing the talent profiles needed for an AI-driven finance workforce. Companies that combine the technology with stronger governance, appropriate talent and reliable data will benefit most.

Article Title: Google rejigs AI leadership as DeepMind CEO shifts role
Article Text:
The shake-up comes during a pivotal juncture for Google DeepMind: the flagship version of its latest Gemini model remains unreleased

Google parent company Alphabet on Wednesday announced a leadership overhaul of its AI division, with AI chief Demis Hassabis leaving his main managerial role and as several leaders of its Gemini model, including veteran engineer Jeff Dean, left the company to launch a startup called Discovery Loop. The shake-up comes during a pivotal juncture for Google DeepMind: the flagship version of its latest Gemini model remains unreleased despite a planned June launch, sparking investor and industry concerns that Google is falling behind its rivals Anthropic and OpenAI, each of which scooped up a star Google AI staffer this summer.Shares of Alphabet fell 4% after the news. Hassabis, a Nobel Prize recipient, will take the newly created title of Alphabet’s chief scientist and transition from being Google DeepMind CEO to being its chairman, he said in a memo to staff.Koray Kavukcuoglu, the unit’s chief technology officer, will assume day-to-day responsibilities of DeepMind in addition to his parallel role as Alphabet’s chief AI architect.
Article Summary: Google parent company Alphabet on Wednesday announced a leadership overhaul of its AI division, with AI chief Demis Hassabis leaving his main managerial role. Hassabis, a Nobel Prize recipient, will take the newly created title of Alphabet’s chief scientist and transition from being Google DeepMind CEO to being its chairman.

Article Title: Before the knowledge walks out the door
Article Text:
Everyone in Silicon Valley is racing to build machines that replace human expertise.

Ahmer Inam

, a schoolteacher's son from Delhi, is building machines that inherit it.

When Ahmer Inam appeared on Fox & Friends in June, his mother watched the segment without following much of it. Her English is limited. There was her son on the famous curved couch of American morning television, fielding questions about artificial intelligence, and she understood almost none of the words. She wept anyway. Some distances need no translation, and the one between a schoolteacher's household in Delhi and a Manhattan television studio is legible in any language.Had she followed the argument, it might have surprised her less than it surprised the audience. Because what Inam was defending, underneath the vocabulary of frontier AI, is approximately the oldest idea in civilisation — the one his father practised for a living: that knowledge survives only when one generation troubles to hand it to the next.Inam has spent twenty-five years building artificial intelligence — long enough to remember when it meant symbolic logic in the late nineties, and senior enough to have run AI and data for Fortune 500 companies, Nike and Wells Fargo among them, back when "chief AI officer" was still an exotic title. He is not, in other words, a critic sniping from the cheap seats. Which makes the thesis of Cognisee, the research lab he founded and leads, sound almost seditious in today's Silicon Valley: "We're not trying to replace the worker," he says."We're trying to make the worker irreplaceable."The problem he is aiming at usually gets filed under the bland heading of "labour shortage." By one estimate, more than two million skilled-trade jobs in the United States could sit unfilled by 2030 — electricians, welders, machinists, the hands America needs if it is serious about building factories, chip plants and grid capacity again. But Inam's diagnosis is sharper than a headcount. "America does not have a work shortage," he likes to say. "It has an expertise shortage."Consider what actually leaves the building when a master electrician retires at sixty-eight. Not the manual — the manual stays. What leaves is the ear that catches a motor running slightly wrong two weeks before it fails; the instinct that connects a faint vibration to a pattern in old maintenance logs; forty years of judgment that was never written down because it could not be. The philosopher Michael Polanyi had a name for this — tacit knowledge, the things we know but cannot tell — and Cognisee is, at bottom, a bet that the most valuable training data on earth is tacit.The company's method has a fable-like symmetry. Its AI begins as an apprentice: it works alongside experienced people and learns what they notice, what they ask, how they make judgment calls. Then it turns around and becomes a coach, carrying that accumulated judgment to the newcomer. "First it's an apprentice," Inam says. "Then it becomes a coach." Picture a 22-year-old on his first aircraft-maintenance job, hearing a sound he has never heard before, with the distilled instincts of the country's best technicians beside him in real time. "He's not being replaced by a machine," Inam says. "He's being mentored by one."The repository where all this lives is called, a little grandly, a Wisdom Vault — a secure library of hard-won know-how from doctors, nurses, electricians, factory workers, farmers, small-business owners. Grand or not, the name gives away the emotional register Inam is working in. This is not pitched as workforce optimisation. It is pitched as inheritance.He is careful — insistent, actually — about the question that framing invites: who owns it? In Cognisee's design, the expert decides what to preserve, what to share, and with whom; the contributor is recognised and rewarded; the knowledge belongs to the person who earned it, not to the machine that absorbed it. "There is a big difference," Inam says, "between being monitored and being mentored." The company is incorporated as a public benefit corporation, which he describes as a legal commitment to the worker rather than a marketing pledge.That ownership principle is also where his quarrel with the reigning AI paradigm becomes explicit. The frontier labs, Inam argues, got intelligent by swallowing the written internet — and the written internet is now substantially swallowed, which is why the industry's plan increasingly amounts to bigger data centres and more electricity, even as some of the field's own pioneers warn of a wall ahead. His contrarian wager is that the next leap will come not from more compute but from the knowledge that never made it onto the internet in the first place — and that it can be gathered by consent rather than by crawler.For an Indian reader, the resonance is hard to miss. This is a country that has watched its weaves, its remedies and its craft knowledge catalogued, carried off and sold back to it before. It is also a country whose deepest teaching traditions were never textual at all, but moved from person to person — the guru-shishya parampara, the ustad and the shagird. Inam has spoken about Wisdom Vaults for indigenous and medicinal knowledge, with communities retaining ownership of what they contribute. One way to describe Cognisee is as an attempt to give the world's oral inheritances an infrastructure layer — sovereignty included.The idea is attracting converts from unexpected quarters. Cognisee's co-founder, Alex Giannou, spent nearly two decades on Wall Street financing precisely the data centres and power deals behind the AI boom; he crossed over, in Inam's telling, because the right bet and the smart bet turned out to be the same one. Among the company's early backers is a senior Google executive who helped invent federated learning, one of the foundational privacy-preserving techniques of modern machine learning. And last year the XPRIZE Foundation, where Inam serves as a Visionary, recognised his work with its Global Visioneering Award.None of which quite explains the conviction. For that you have to go back to Delhi. Inam grew up in a low-income household, the son of a teacher — a man who spent his working life on the least scalable expertise-transfer technology ever devised: one adult, one room, one generation at a time. The son's journey to America was not gilded; there were stretches, early on, when he could not always afford to eat. It takes a particular kind of person to emerge from that and conclude that a nation's most undervalued asset sits not in its server farms but in the heads of its retiring machinists and nurses."Every generation should start where the last one left off," Inam says. It sounds like a product principle. It is closer to a family creed — the thing his father practised without ever calling it a thesis, the thing his mother recognised on a television screen in a language she does not speak. Some knowledge, it turns out, transfers just fine.
Article Summary: Ahmer Inam, a schoolteacher's son from Delhi, is building machines that inherit it. The problem he is aiming at usually gets filed under the bland heading of "labour shortage" By one estimate, more than two million skilled-trade jobs in the United States could sit unfilled by 2030.

Article Title: 'Turned it in…': Google's 30th employee Jeff Dean posts photo of everything he handed back on his last day at Google after 27 years
Article Text:
The stickers on Jeff Dean's laptop are a working history of Google AI

What Jeff Dean's farewell email to Google employees actually said

Jeff Dean's final act as a Google employee was a photograph. On Friday, the man who joined the company as employee number 30 in 1999 posted a picture of the two things he surrendered on his way out the door: a scuffed black Google laptop, and the plastic-sleeved badge with his face on it, still marked FTE. The caption ran to three words.The post has since crossed 2.8 million views, which tells you something about how closely the industry has been watching this particular exit. It comes days after Google announced a sweeping AI leadership reshuffle that moved Demis Hassabis out of the Google DeepMind CEO role and into a chair position, with CTO Koray Kavukcuoglu stepping up as SVP. Dean is leaving alongside Sanjay Ghemawat, Oriol Vinyals and Quoc Le to co-found Discovery Loop, a public benefit corporation backed by Alphabet, Radical Ventures and Khosla Ventures.The laptop is the better artefact, and it appears to be a Chromebook, a modest daily driver for the man who built Google's AI infrastructure. Its lid carries a rainbow-sliced anatomical brain, the old Google Brain logo, a TensorFlow decal, a sticker from something called the Optic Nerve 2020 Summit, a tiny Android figure, and a hand-drawn cartoon of a very large table with the words "BIG TABLE" scrawled underneath.Dean co-created BigTable. He co-authored TensorFlow. He founded Google Brain in 2011.Nearly every sticker on that lid is a thing he built, which is either charming or slightly unhinged depending on your view of engineer merch.When one user asked whether he had really kept the same machine for six years, Dean replied that he thought so, maybe five. Google's chief scientist, apparently, does not chase hardware refresh cycles.Dean also shared the internal note he sent colleagues, and it reads less like a resignation than an inventory. He listed growing Search's index 100 times over and its query rate 1,000 times. Building the first Google Ads system. Launching Google News and Translate. MapReduce, Spanner, DistBelief, Pathways. Starting the TPU programme. Kicking off Gemini with Vinyals as co-tech-lead.Then the smaller stuff, which is the part people are actually sharing: biking to offsites in Monterey, the "Run or Else…" group runs, changing desks 18 times, and visiting 29 Google offices across five continents. He noted that a Google badge could get you a cappuccino in more than 100 cities. That badge is now in a photograph.Dean will be CEO at Discovery Loop, which plans to automate the experimental loop itself, running thousands of AI-designed experiments in parallel across machine learning, chip design and drug discovery. Sundar Pichai called it a privilege to have worked alongside Dean and Ghemawat, and Alphabet is providing compute for the first year.Inside Google, employees reacted mostly with memes. One line summed up the mood well: Google isn't losing Jeff Dean, it's open-sourcing him.
Article Summary: Jeff Dean is leaving Google to co-found Discovery Loop. He joined the company as employee number 30 in 1999. Dean shared a picture of his laptop and badge on his way out the door. The post has since crossed 2.8 million views.

Article Title: Job listings show Nvidia hiring for a new AI safety team to address one of the biggest ‘AI threats’
Article Text:
Focus on autonomous agents and software patching

“rooted in the firm belief that open-weight models, transparency, and broad scientific scrutiny are foundational to American AI leadership and cybersecurity defense.”

Nvidia advocates for open-source security

Nvidia is reportedly assembling a dedicated AI safety and security engineering team, as per a series of corporate job listings posted late last month. The hiring initiative signals a broader effort by the chipmaker to address security vulnerabilities and safety risks associated with autonomous AI agents, which are currently seen as one of the biggest threats of technology, and open-weight models before they reach widespread commercial deployment.According to the disclosures (spotted by Business Insider), Nvidia is recruiting an engineer to serve as the “founding technical leader” for the new team, alongside roles for a security research engineer, an evaluation engineer and a senior engineering manager.The primary responsibility of the newly-formed division is said to be evaluating autonomous AI agents prior to deployment, testing their operational limits and developing AI-powered security software to automatically detect and patch code vulnerabilities.One job description notes that the team’s mission isUnlike “closed” proprietary software, open-weight models make their trained parameters publicly accessible for inspection and fine-tuning, allowing outside developers and researchers to evaluate how the software operates.The internal safety push aligns with Nvidia’s broader public strategy advocating for open-weight AI development, positioning the company alongside alternative approaches to closed ecosystems built by competitors like OpenAI and Anthropic.In a recent public letter addressed to US policymakers, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang urged government support for open AI models, arguing that open architectures strengthen overall software resilience and national cybersecurity.Additionally, Nvidia recently became a founding member of the Open Secure AI Alliance, which is a consortium of 120 companies, including Microsoft, Palantir, SpaceX, and Hugging Face, focused on developing open-source security defenses for machine learning applications.
Article Summary: N Nvidia is reportedly assembling a dedicated AI safety and security engineering team. The hiring initiative signals a broader effort by the chipmaker to address security vulnerabilities and safety risks associated with autonomous AI agents. The internal safety push aligns with Nvidia’s broader public strategy advocating for open-weight AI development.
